limitations: The opinion addresses discovery obligations and does not establish that the facial-recognition result was false or that the detention was wrongful.

summary: New Jersey's published appellate opinion records that an initial NJROIC facial-recognition search found no match, after which NYPD's Real Time Crime Center offered Francisco Arteaga as a possible match from the raw video. Police then used that photo in arrays shown to two eyewitnesses, who identified Arteaga, and he was charged. Arteaga later sought detailed discovery concerning the facial-recognition process. VIGIL records the evidentiary and contestability pathway without treating the court opinion as a finding that the facial-recognition result was false or that his detention was wrongful.

assessment_boundaries: VIGIL does not describe Arteaga as wrongfully arrested or the facial-recognition result as false on the basis of the appellate opinion.
The eyewitness identifications are preserved as part of the evidentiary sequence; the record does not assume they were wholly independent of the earlier machine-generated candidate.
The taxonomy mapping addresses the authority afforded to inferential identity evidence and its downstream evidentiary role, not Arteaga's guilt or innocence.
vigil_assessment.factual_basis: The New Jersey Appellate Division records that NJROIC first found no facial-recognition match from a still image. Police then sent the raw video to the NYPD Real Time Crime Center, where a detective captured a still, compared it against databases and offered Francisco Arteaga as a possible match. Police subsequently included the resulting photo with five fillers in arrays shown to two eyewitnesses; both identified Arteaga, and he was charged. Arteaga later sought thirteen categories of discovery concerning the facial-recognition process. The opinion does not establish that the match was false or that his detention was wrongful.
vigil_assessment.governance_interpretation: This occurrence shows why inferential-authority governance includes evidentiary lineage and contestability. A first no-match followed by a possible match from a different system is materially relevant to how confidence should be calibrated. Once that possible match structures photo arrays and downstream witness identifications, later evidence may no longer be wholly independent of the originating inference. The defendant's discovery requests therefore concern the ability to test the reliability, method and provenance of evidence that materially shaped the investigative pathway.
vigil_assessment.significance_to_cam: INC-000008 is valuable because it demonstrates that the governance problem can exist even without a judicial finding that the biometric inference was wrong. Consequential use of an AI-derived identity lead requires provenance and disclosure sufficient for the affected person and decision-maker to test how the inference entered and structured the evidence chain.
